title: Circles, Arcs & Sectors
coreInsight: The radius controls a circle's metric structure; circumference and area scale differently, while arcs and sectors represent fractions determined by central angle.
targetLearnerRealization: Radius determines circle boundary and coverage differently, while a central angle selects the same fraction of a circle's arc and area as it does of 360°.
learningObjectives: Interpret circumference as boundary length and area as square-unit coverage.
Explain why doubling radius doubles circumference but quadruples area.
Find arc and sector fractions from central angles.
Subtract concentric circle areas and coordinate circle geometry with right triangles.

continuity.openingCallback: Separate a region's boundary from its interior before measuring a curved shape.
closingSeeds: Area fractions inside a circle can become probabilities when a random point is chosen.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Radius and diameter can be interchanged.
Circumference and area are the same type of measurement.
A sector fraction depends on the radius rather than the central angle fraction.

beats.purpose: Separate circle boundary and coverage before formulas become interchangeable symbols.
beats.expectedRealization: A radius-3 circle has circumference 6π linear units and area 9π square units.
beats.transitionIn: A rectangle needed one measure around and another inside. Replace its straight boundary with a curved rim.
beats.whyNow: The paired tire-track and paint context preserves G3's distinction while introducing radius-controlled formulas.
beats.entryBridge: Decide which quantity traces the rim and which fills the disc.
beats.exitBridge: The same radius enters once for circumference and twice for area.
learnerPrompts: Which expression measures one trip around the rim, and which measures the covered disc?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Circumference is 6π units and area is 9π square units.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Boundary uses C=2πr; coverage uses A=πr², with different units.

visual.ariaLabel: Circle rim measured as six pi linear units and disc measured as nine pi square units

steps.title: Unwrap the rim
steps.body: Circumference is π diameters long: C=πd=2πr.

steps.title: Cover the disc
steps.body: Circle area scales with the square of radius: A=πr².

resolution.takeaway: Circumference measures curved boundary; area measures interior coverage.

beats.purpose: Attach radius and diameter to precise center-based segments.
beats.expectedRealization: Diameter crosses the center between two circle points and equals two radii.
beats.transitionIn: Both formulas use a center-to-rim distance. Extend that segment straight through the center.
beats.prompt: A circle has diameter 14 cm. What is its radius?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The diameter is two radii, so r=7 cm.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The center splits a diameter into two equal radius segments.

resolution.takeaway: Radius is center to rim; diameter is rim to rim through the center.

beats.purpose: Derive distinct scaling behavior for boundary and area.
beats.expectedRealization: Doubling radius multiplies circumference by 2 and area by 4.
beats.transitionIn: Grow the radius from r to 2r and track each formula's copies of r.
beats.prompt: When a circle's radius doubles, what happens to its circumference and area?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Boundary has one radius factor; area has two.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compare 2π(2r) with 2πr, then π(2r)² with πr².

resolution.takeaway: Radius scales boundary linearly and coverage quadratically.

beats.purpose: Build arc and sector formulas from fraction of a full turn.
beats.expectedRealization: A 90° central angle selects one quarter of any concentric circle, regardless of radius.
beats.transitionIn: Hold radius fixed and turn one bounding ray through part of 360°.
beats.prompt: A sector has central angle 90°. What fraction of its circle's circumference and area does it contain?

options.text: One quarter of circumference but one half of area

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. 90/360=1/4 selects one quarter of arc and sector area.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compare the central turn with the full 360° turn.

steps.body: Arc length=(90/360)C and sector area=(90/360)A. Radius changes the whole sizes, not the selected fraction.

resolution.takeaway: Central angle fraction controls both arc and sector.

beats.purpose: Name circle formulas and fraction relationships after their measurement meanings are established.
beats.expectedRealization: Each formula records a different object and dimension.
beats.name: Circle, arc, and sector measures
beats.conciseDefinition: For radius r and diameter d=2r, circumference C=2πr measures boundary and area A=πr² measures coverage. A central angle θ selects θ/360 of both circumference and area.
beats.memoryHook: Rim once, disc squared, angle over 360.

beats.purpose: Combine a tangent-created right triangle with subtraction of circle areas.
beats.expectedRealization: The half-chord is 8, the inner radius is 6, and the annulus area is π(10²−6²)=64π.
beats.transitionIn: Two concentric circles create a region measured by outer disc minus inner disc. A tangent chord hides the inner radius inside a right triangle.
beats.whyNow: The learner can distinguish circle area from boundary and can reactivate G5 to recover an unknown radius.
beats.entryBridge: Bisect the chord, use the perpendicular radius, then subtract disc areas.
beats.exitBridge: The radius squares differ by 64, so the annulus area is 64π.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Concentric circles with radial area bands.
learnerPrompts: Why is the 16-unit chord split into two 8-unit halves?
Which right triangle contains the inner radius?
How does the difference of radius squares give annulus area?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The inner radius is 6 and the annulus area is 64π.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use half-chord 8 with outer radius 10 as a hypotenuse, then subtract the two disc areas.

steps.title: Build the right triangle
steps.body: The perpendicular center-to-chord segment bisects 16, so the half-chord is 8.

resolution.takeaway: An annulus is outer circle area minus inner circle area.

beats.purpose: Coordinate difference-of-squares ring areas with a central-angle fraction and balance condition.
beats.expectedRealization: The middle ring contributes 3π; the outer sector must provide 1.5π of its 5π ring, or 3/10 of 360°=108°.
beats.transitionIn: The annulus used a whole ring. Now shade one ring completely and only a central-angle fraction of another.
beats.whyNow: The learner understands ring subtraction and sector fractions, so the balance condition can coordinate both without formula confusion.
beats.entryBridge: Find all ring areas, determine half the full disc, fill the shortfall from the outer ring, then convert its fraction to degrees.
beats.exitBridge: A 3/10 share of the outer ring requires the same 3/10 share of a full turn: 108°.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Concentric circles with radial bands and a central-angle sector.
learnerPrompts: What are the three radial band areas?
How much shaded area is needed beyond the full middle ring?
What fraction of the outer ring is 1.5π out of 5π?
What central angle selects that fraction?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The sector is 3/10 of a full turn, so the angle is 108°.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Balance half of the 9π disc: after the 3π middle ring, the outer-ring sector must supply 1.5π.

steps.title: Measure the bands
steps.body: The disc and rings have areas π, 3π, and 5π; total area is 9π.

steps.title: Find the sector's job
steps.body: Half the disc is 4.5π. With 3π already shaded, the sector must add 1.5π.

resolution.takeaway: A central angle selects the same fraction of an annular band as of a full turn.

beats.whyNow: Return to one circle after layered regions.
beats.entryBridge: Halve the diameter before using a radius formula, or use C=πd directly.
learnerPrompts: Is the given segment a radius or diameter?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use C=πd with d=18, or r=9 in C=2πr.

resolution.takeaway: Read the segment role before substituting.

beats.purpose: Assess circumference and area with correct units.
beats.whyNow: Compute both quantities from the same radius without mixing them.
beats.entryBridge: Use one radius factor for rim and two for disc.
learnerPrompts: Which result needs linear units and which needs square units?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Circumference is 10π cm and area is 25π cm².

resolution.takeaway: Formula and unit both identify the measured object.

beats.entryBridge: Reduce 72/360 before multiplying the full area.
learnerPrompts: What fraction of a full turn is 72°?

resolution.takeaway: Angle fraction, not radius, chooses the share.

beats.purpose: Assess radius scaling on circumference and area.
beats.whyNow: Use a fractional scale to avoid relying on doubling memory.
beats.entryBridge: Apply k to boundary and k² to coverage.
beats.exitBridge: Tripling radius makes area nine times larger.
learnerPrompts: How many radius factors appear in area?
beats.incorrectFeedback: A=πr², so replacing r by 3r introduces 3².

steps.body: π(3r)²=9πr², so the area factor is 9.

beats.purpose: Assess combined ring subtraction and sector fraction.
beats.whyNow: Finish with the two core operations in one compact problem.
beats.entryBridge: Find the whole annulus first, then take the angle share.
beats.exitBridge: The annulus is 48π and one quarter is 12π.
learnerPrompts: What is the ring's full area before selecting the 90° sector?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The annular sector area is 12π.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compute π(8²−4²), then take 90/360 of it.

steps.body: Annulus area=π(64−16)=48π. A 90° sector is one quarter, so area=12π.

resolution.takeaway: Build the whole region before taking its central-angle fraction.

beats.purpose: Consolidate roles, dimension, scaling, and angle fractions.
beats.expectedRealization: Circle problems become stable when the whole region and measurement type are named first.
beats.transitionIn: Rims, discs, rings, chords, and sectors all depended on identifying the measured object before calculating.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable circle routine? Select all four.

options.text: Distinguish boundary length from square-unit area.
Build a full disc or annulus before taking a sector fraction.
Use central angle divided by 360 for arc or sector share.

response.feedback: Each action protects a different circle quantity.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Name the segment, measurement, whole region, and angular share.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four are needed to prevent radius, unit, or fraction mix-ups.

steps.body: Circle formulas are compact descriptions of objects: a center-to-rim length, a curved boundary, a covered disc, or an angular fraction of either.

resolution.takeaway: Identify the object first; then radius, dimension, and angle determine the calculation.

beats.purpose: Connect sector area fractions to later geometric probability.
beats.expectedRealization: Uniform random area makes probability equal to favorable-area fraction.
beats.transitionIn: A 72° sector occupied one fifth of its circle regardless of radius.
beats.prompt: If a point is chosen uniformly from a disc, why might the chance it lands in a sector equal the sector's central-angle fraction?
beats.takeaway: When every equal area is equally likely, geometric probability becomes an area ratio.

notes: Design: G3's boundary/coverage distinction becomes circumference versus disc area. Radius/diameter roles precede scaling, and central-angle shares are derived from fraction of a full turn. The guided annulus reuses right triangles; the transfer balances whole-ring and sector areas.

Beat outline: rim-versus-disc anchor -> radius/diameter -> radius scaling -> central-angle fraction -> name -> authentic annulus -> authentic concentric sector -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> probability hook.
Both mapped animations are referenced unchanged after submission over their full timelines. Existing generic choice-grid visuals suffice; no renderer or animation source changes were made.
Generated results were verified by both formula substitution and independent scale, fraction-of-turn, or difference-of-squares audits. The lesson remains draft pending human review.
